title: Epicurus: Pleasure, Friendship and Freedom from Fear
subtitle: Bread, water, good friends and no fear of death: the surprisingly modest philosophy of pleasure
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain why Epicurus made pleasure the goal of life and why his idea of pleasure is so different from indulgence
Classify desires using Epicurus' three categories and explain the goal of ataraxia
Reconstruct Epicurus' argument that death is nothing to us and Lucretius' symmetry argument, and assess objections to both
Describe the community of the Garden, the role of friendship and the atomist physics behind Epicurean ethics, including the swerve
Apply Epicurean ideas to modern research on happiness, consumption and fear
hook:
Around 306 BCE, a man from the island of Samos bought a house with a garden just outside the walls of Athens. It became one of the strangest communities in the ancient world. Men and women lived and studied there together, along with at least one enslaved man who was treated as a fellow student. Their diet was mostly bread and water. On special occasions, someone might send for a little pot of cheese. And their founder taught, without embarrassment, that the goal of life is **pleasure**.

Today the word *epicure* means someone devoted to fine food and wine, and 'Epicurean' suggests luxury. Epicurus would have been horrified. His philosophy of pleasure is closer to the art of needing very little, fearing nothing and spending your days with friends. Yesterday the Cynics told us that convention makes us miserable. Today Epicurus offers a gentler diagnosis: we are unhappy because we fear the wrong things and want the wrong things. Fix those, he says, and happiness is easy.

sections.heading: Epicurus and the Garden
sections.body:
**Epicurus** was born in 341 BCE on Samos, to Athenian parents who had settled there. He later said he began doing philosophy at around fourteen, when a teacher reading a poem about the origin of the world could not explain where Chaos itself had come from. As a young man he studied with Nausiphanes, a follower of Democritus, whose atomism you met on Day 7. After teaching in Mytilene and Lampsacus, he moved to Athens and bought the property that gave his school its name: **the Garden**.

The Garden was not a public lecture hall like Plato's Academy or Aristotle's Lyceum but something closer to a community of friends. Unusually for its time, it welcomed women, including Leontion and Themista, who are named in the sources as students, and enslaved people such as Mys, whom Epicurus freed in his will. Members memorised short summaries of the teaching so they could carry the cure with them. The Roman philosopher Seneca, who was not an Epicurean, reports the welcome said to be written over the gate: roughly, stranger, you will do well to stay here, where the highest good is pleasure.

Epicurus wrote a great deal, including a work *On Nature* in thirty-seven books, but most is lost. What we have is precious: three letters summarising his views, preserved by Diogenes Laertius; the *Principal Doctrines*, forty short maxims; a further collection called the *Vatican Sayings*, discovered in a Vatican manuscript in 1888; and charred fragments of *On Nature* found among the papyrus scrolls buried by Vesuvius at Herculaneum in 79 CE. In the second century CE, a wealthy Epicurean named Diogenes of Oenoanda even carved a summary of the teaching on a huge stone wall in his town in what is now Turkey, so that passers-by could be cured.

Epicurus died in 270 BCE after a painful illness, probably kidney stones. In a letter written on his last day, he described it as a happy day, because the memory of his philosophical conversations outweighed his physical suffering.

sections.heading: What Pleasure Really Means
sections.body:
Epicurus' starting point is simple and hard to deny. Every animal, from birth, seeks pleasure and avoids pain. Pleasure, he concluded, is the beginning and end of the happy life, the natural good. Philosophers call this **hedonism**, from the Greek *hedone*, pleasure.

But what kind of pleasure? Here Epicurus surprises us. In his *Letter to Menoeceus* he says plainly that when he calls pleasure the goal, he does not mean the pleasures of the profligate or of sensuality, as some ignorant or hostile people think. He means the absence of pain in the body and of trouble in the soul. Endless drinking parties and feasts do not make a pleasant life; sober reasoning does.

Epicurus distinguished two kinds of pleasure. **Kinetic** pleasures are pleasures of motion: the enjoyable process of eating when hungry or drinking when thirsty. **Katastematic** or 'static' pleasures are the pleasure of being in a settled, satisfied state: not hungry, not in pain, not anxious. For Epicurus, the highest pleasure is the static kind. In the body it is **aponia**, freedom from pain; in the mind it is **ataraxia**, tranquillity or freedom from disturbance.

This leads to a striking claim: once pain is removed, pleasure cannot be increased, only varied. A gourmet feast does not make you more satisfied than bread when you are hungry; it only varies the pleasure. So the luxurious life gives you no more of what really matters than a simple one, and it brings extra risks: expense, dependence, anxiety and illness.

Epicurus was also no simple-minded pleasure-maximiser. He taught that we should sometimes choose pain, like an unpleasant medical treatment, for the sake of greater pleasure later, and sometimes refuse a pleasure that brings greater pain. Doing this well requires **prudence** (*phronesis*), which he called more precious than philosophy itself. And he insisted that it is impossible to live pleasantly without living wisely, honourably and justly. Virtue, for Epicurus, is not the goal, as it will be for the Stoics. It is the indispensable means to a pleasant life.

sections.heading: Three Kinds of Desire
sections.body:
If pleasure is the goal, why are so many people unhappy? Because, Epicurus says, they misunderstand their own desires. He sorted desires into three groups.

1. **Natural and necessary** desires: for food, drink, shelter, and the friendship and philosophy we need for a happy life. These are easy to satisfy and painful to ignore.
2. **Natural but unnecessary** desires: for gourmet food, fine wine, sex, comfortable furniture. These are natural variations on real needs. They are fine to enjoy when they come easily, but we should not depend on them.
3. **Empty** or vain desires: for wealth, fame, power, luxury, immortality. These are produced by false opinions, and they have no natural limit. However much money or fame you have, you can always want more, so these desires can never be satisfied.

The practical lesson is that happiness lies in limiting desire, not endlessly satisfying it. A saying attributed to Epicurus by later anthologists makes the point: if you want to make someone rich, do not add to their money but subtract from their desires. Epicurus claimed that with bread and water he could rival Zeus himself in happiness.

This also explains Epicurus' political advice, which sounds unusual after Aristotle. Seeking power and fame is an empty desire that brings enemies, anxiety and danger. So Epicurus advised his followers to avoid public life where possible. A slogan associated with the school was **live unnoticed** (*lathe biosas*). Critics like Plutarch attacked this as selfish withdrawal. Epicureans replied that they were not anti-social, simply choosing a safer and kinder form of community: friendship.

Friendship was central. One of the *Principal Doctrines* says that of all the things wisdom provides for the happiness of the whole of life, by far the greatest is the possession of friendship. Epicureans debated whether friendship begins in usefulness, and many held that it begins there but becomes valued for its own sake. Either way, a life without friends was, for Epicurus, a life exposed and afraid.

sections.heading: Atoms, Gods and the Fourfold Cure
sections.body:
Why did a philosophy of happiness need physics? Because, Epicurus believed, the two great fears that poison human life are fear of the gods and fear of death, and both rest on false beliefs about how the world works.

Epicurus adopted and adapted the **atomism** of Leucippus and Democritus (Day 7). Everything that exists is made of tiny, indivisible atoms moving in an infinite void. Worlds form and dissolve through atoms colliding and combining. No divine plan is needed. Thunder, earthquakes and plagues have natural causes, not angry gods behind them.

Epicurus was not an atheist. He believed gods exist, perfectly blessed and immortal. But precisely because they are perfectly happy, they have no troubles and do not trouble anyone else. They do not reward or punish us, and we need not fear them. (A famous argument about evil, asking how an all-powerful, all-good god could allow suffering, is often attributed to Epicurus, but the attribution comes from the Christian writer Lactantius, centuries later, and is doubtful.)

Later Epicureans summed up the whole therapy in four lines, known as the **tetrapharmakos**, the 'fourfold remedy', preserved in a papyrus by the Epicurean Philodemus. In paraphrase:

> God is nothing to fear; death is nothing to worry about; the good is easy to get; the terrible is easy to endure.

The last line needs explaining. Epicurus argued that severe pain is usually brief, and long-lasting pain is usually mild enough to bear, especially when balanced by pleasant memories, as on his own deathbed.

There was one problem with Democritus' atomism, as Epicurus saw it. If atoms simply fall straight down through the void at the same speed, they would never collide, and nothing would form. Worse, if every atom's motion is fixed by previous motions, then human choices are fixed too, and we are not free. The Epicurean solution was the **swerve**: occasionally, at no fixed time or place, an atom deviates from its path by the smallest possible amount. This makes collisions possible and breaks the chain of fate, leaving room for free will. Our clearest account of the swerve comes from Lucretius, who called it the *clinamen*. Critics, ancient and modern, have objected that a random swerve does not obviously give us *free* choice, only unpredictable motion. You will meet this debate again whenever philosophers discuss determinism.

sections.heading: Death Is Nothing to Us
sections.body:
Epicurus' most famous argument concerns death. In the *Letter to Menoeceus* he writes that we should accustom ourselves to believing that **death is nothing to us**, because all good and evil lie in sensation, and death is the end of sensation. In a well-known line from the same letter: death, the most frightening of evils, is nothing to us, since when we exist death is not present, and when death is present we no longer exist.

Lay the argument out step by step.

1. Something can be bad for you only if you can experience it.
2. When you are dead, you experience nothing, because the atoms of your soul have scattered.
3. So being dead cannot be bad for you.
4. So it is irrational to fear being dead.

The **Roman poet Lucretius** (c. 99–55 BCE) added a second argument in his great poem *On the Nature of Things* (*De Rerum Natura*), a six-book presentation of Epicurean philosophy in Latin verse. Look back, he says, at the endless ages before you were born. They did not trouble you at all. The time after your death is a mirror held up to that earlier time. If you are not distressed by your non-existence before birth, why be distressed by your non-existence after death? This is called the **symmetry argument**.

Notice what Epicurus is and is not claiming. He does not say that the process of dying cannot be painful, or that we should not grieve for others. His target is the dread of being dead, which he thought poisoned whole lives and drove people to superstition, greed and violence.

There are strong objections. The modern philosopher Thomas Nagel argued in his essay 'Death' (1970) that death can be bad for us even if we never experience it, because it deprives us of the goods we would otherwise have had, just as being betrayed behind your back is bad for you even if you never find out. Others answer Lucretius by noting an asymmetry: the future is where our plans, projects and loves are directed, while the past before birth contained nothing of ours to lose. Philosophers still argue about whether Epicurus can be rescued. Even his critics admit that the argument forces us to say exactly what it is about death that we fear.

sections.heading: Reputation and Legacy
sections.body:
Few philosophers have been misrepresented as often as Epicurus. Already in his lifetime, critics spread stories of gluttony and debauchery, which Diogenes Laertius records and rejects. Stoics accused Epicureans of being selfish and lazy. Later, Christian writers condemned the school for denying divine providence and the immortality of the soul. Over time, 'Epicurean' came to mean a lover of luxury, the opposite of what the Garden practised.

Yet the school was remarkably long-lived and loyal. Epicureans celebrated their founder's memory with monthly gatherings, and the school continued for centuries. In Rome, Lucretius' poem became one of the masterpieces of Latin literature. Then it nearly vanished. In 1417, the Italian humanist Poggio Bracciolini found a manuscript of *On the Nature of Things* in a German monastery, and the poem's atomism and calm materialism began to circulate again in Renaissance Europe, a story you will connect with Days 38 and 41. Thomas Jefferson later declared himself an Epicurean in a letter.

Compare Epicurus with yesterday's Cynics. Both prize simplicity and independence. But where Diogenes sought hardship and provocation, Epicurus sought comfort in its simplest form and the quiet company of friends. And compare him with tomorrow's Stoics, his great rivals. Both promised tranquillity. But the Stoics would insist that virtue is the only good and that pleasure is merely an 'indifferent', while Epicurus held that virtue is valuable only because it leads to a pleasant life. That disagreement, between a life organised around pleasure and a life organised around virtue, runs right through the history of ethics, from Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism (Day 61) to modern debates about well-being.

keyQuote.source: Epicurus, Principal Doctrines 2 and Letter to Menoeceus

modernConnection.title: The Hedonic Treadmill and the Science of Enough
modernConnection.body:
Modern psychology has rediscovered Epicurus' theory of desire under a new name: the **hedonic treadmill**. In a famous 1978 study, Philip Brickman and colleagues compared lottery winners with ordinary people and found that the winners were not much happier, and took less pleasure in everyday activities. Later research on 'hedonic adaptation' has shown that we quickly get used to most gains, such as a raise, a bigger house or a new car, and our happiness drifts back toward where it was. Epicurus would nod: empty desires have no natural limit, so satisfying them only resets the target.

Other findings also sound Epicurean. The Harvard Study of Adult Development, which has followed its participants since 1938, has found that the quality of close relationships is one of the strongest predictors of health and happiness in old age, more than wealth or fame. Studies by Leaf Van Boven and Thomas Gilovich suggest that spending on experiences tends to bring more lasting happiness than spending on possessions, and work by Elizabeth Dunn and colleagues finds that spending on other people often beats spending on ourselves. 'The greatest of all goods is friendship' is not a bad headline for this research.

Epicurus' therapy for fear also has modern parallels. Terror management theory, developed by social psychologists in the 1980s, argues that much human behaviour, from status-seeking to hostility toward outsiders, is driven by an often unconscious fear of death. Epicurus made almost the same diagnosis: fear of death drives greed and violence.

But the comparison has limits. Psychologists measure happiness with surveys of life satisfaction and positive feeling, whereas Epicurus' ataraxia is a specific state of calm that may not show up on a questionnaire. Some modern research also suggests that meaning and engagement, not only tranquillity, matter to a good life, which is closer to Aristotle (Day 20). And Epicurus' advice to 'live unnoticed' fits awkwardly with problems that need collective action. You cannot retreat to a garden from climate change or a pandemic. A modern Epicurean has to ask whether tranquillity can ever be a purely private achievement.

vocabulary.definition: The view that pleasure is the highest good and the goal of life; for Epicurus, pleasure understood mainly as the absence of pain and disturbance.
vocabulary.example: Epicurus' hedonism recommended bread, water and friends, not wild parties.

vocabulary.definition: Tranquillity of mind; freedom from mental disturbance, fear and anxiety, which Epicurus considered the highest pleasure of the soul.
vocabulary.example: After accepting that her exam result was out of her hands, she felt a kind of ataraxia for the first time all week.

vocabulary.definition: Freedom from bodily pain; together with ataraxia, it makes up the Epicurean goal of a pleasant life.
vocabulary.example: For Epicurus, a person who is not hungry, cold or sick already enjoys aponia, the highest bodily pleasure.

vocabulary.definition: Kinetic pleasures come from an activity of satisfying a need (like eating when hungry); katastematic or static pleasures are the settled state of being satisfied and untroubled, which Epicurus valued most.
vocabulary.example: The first bite of lunch gives kinetic pleasure; the calm contentment of not being hungry afterwards is katastematic.

vocabulary.definition: In Epicurus' classification, desires that are neither natural nor necessary, such as for fame, power or great wealth; they arise from false opinions and have no natural limit.
vocabulary.example: Wanting a thousand more followers after already gaining ten thousand is a classic empty desire.

vocabulary.definition: The 'fourfold remedy' summarising Epicurean therapy: the gods are not to be feared, death is nothing to worry about, the good is easy to get, and the terrible is easy to endure.
vocabulary.example: Epicureans memorised the tetrapharmakos so they could repeat it whenever anxiety struck.

vocabulary.definition: The tiny, unpredictable deviation of atoms from their paths, posited by the Epicureans to explain collisions and to make room for free will; best described by Lucretius.
vocabulary.example: Without the swerve, Lucretius argued, atoms would fall forever in parallel lines and nothing would ever form.

vocabulary.definition: Lucretius' argument that the time after our death is a mirror image of the time before our birth, so we should no more fear the one than we regret the other.
vocabulary.example: The symmetry argument asks why you are untroubled that you missed the Roman Empire, yet troubled that you will miss the twenty-fourth century.

thinkingExercise.title: An Epicurean Audit of Your Desires
thinkingExercise.prompt: Use Epicurus' three categories of desire to examine your own wants, and then test his argument about death against your own feelings.
steps: Write down ten things you currently want, large or small (for example, a holiday, a promotion, more sleep, a new jacket, more followers, a closer friendship).
Sort them into Epicurus' three groups: natural and necessary, natural but unnecessary, and empty. Which group is the longest?
Choose one empty desire. What false belief might be producing it? Imagine you subtracted the desire rather than satisfying it. What would change?

Now consider Epicurus' claim that death is nothing to us. Write down honestly what, if anything, you fear about death. Is it being dead, the process of dying, leaving others, or missing out on the future?
Decide whether Epicurus' argument or Nagel's deprivation reply better fits the fear you identified, and explain why in three or four sentences.

summary: Epicurus (341–270 BCE) founded the Garden in Athens, a community of friends that included women and enslaved people, and taught that pleasure is the goal of life.
By pleasure he meant mainly aponia (no bodily pain) and ataraxia (tranquillity), not luxury; once pain is removed, pleasure can only be varied, not increased.
He divided desires into natural and necessary, natural but unnecessary, and empty; happiness comes from limiting desires and from friendship, the greatest good wisdom provides.
Atomist physics frees us from fear of the gods, who exist but do not interfere; the swerve, described by Lucretius, explains collisions and leaves room for free will.
Death is nothing to us because where death is, we are not; Lucretius added the symmetry argument, while critics like Nagel argue death harms us by deprivation.
Though 'epicurean' now suggests luxury, the real Epicurus taught a simple life, and his ideas echo in modern research on hedonic adaptation and relationships.

quiz.question: What did Epicurus mean by pleasure as the goal of life?
options: The greatest possible intensity of sensual enjoyment
The pleasures of fame and political success
Pleasure received from the gods as a reward for piety
Above all, the absence of pain in the body and of disturbance in the mind
quiz.explanation: In the Letter to Menoeceus, Epicurus explicitly rejects the pleasures of the profligate and defines the goal as aponia and ataraxia.

quiz.question: According to Epicurus, which of these is an empty desire?
options: The desire for water when thirsty
The desire to become the most famous person in the city
The desire for a tasty meal
The desire for friendship
quiz.explanation: Fame is neither natural nor necessary; it comes from false opinion and has no natural limit. Water is natural and necessary, a tasty meal natural but unnecessary, and friendship essential to happiness.

quiz.question: What is the core of Epicurus' argument that death is nothing to us?
options: The soul is immortal, so death is only a passage to a better life
The gods will reward the virtuous after death
Good and bad lie in sensation, and when we are dead we have no sensation
Death is natural, so it must be good
quiz.explanation: Since all good and evil require sensation and death is the end of sensation, being dead cannot be bad for the one who is dead. Epicurus denied the soul's survival.

quiz.question: Why did the Epicureans introduce the 'swerve' of atoms?
options: To explain how atoms collide to form worlds and to leave room for free will
To prove that the gods guide the motion of atoms
To explain why atoms are invisible
To show that the void does not exist
quiz.explanation: Without some deviation, atoms falling in parallel would never collide, and every motion would be fixed by earlier ones. The swerve solves both problems, though critics doubt randomness amounts to freedom.

quiz.question: A person wins a large sum of money, buys a bigger house, and a year later feels about as happy as before. Which Epicurean idea does this modern finding best support?
options: The symmetry argument
The tetrapharmakos's claim that the gods are not to be feared
The swerve
The claim that once pain is removed, pleasure cannot be increased, and that desires for wealth have no natural limit
quiz.explanation: Hedonic adaptation matches Epicurus' view that luxury only varies pleasure and that empty desires keep resetting their targets.

quiz.question: What is Lucretius' symmetry argument?
options: Pleasure and pain are always equal in a life, so they cancel out
The non-existence after death mirrors the non-existence before birth, which does not trouble us, so death should not trouble us either
Every atom has a matching atom on the other side of the universe
Friendship is valuable because both friends benefit equally
quiz.explanation: In On the Nature of Things, Book III, Lucretius compares the time after death with the time before birth to argue that fear of death is irrational.

quiz.question: How did Epicurus' view of virtue differ from that of his Stoic rivals?
options: Epicurus thought virtue was irrelevant to happiness
Epicurus thought virtue was the only good, while the Stoics valued pleasure
Epicurus valued virtue as the indispensable means to a pleasant life, while the Stoics held virtue to be the only good
They agreed completely about virtue and differed only in physics
quiz.explanation: Epicurus said you cannot live pleasantly without living wisely and justly, but pleasure remained the goal. The Stoics, as you will see on Day 25, made virtue itself the only good.

quiz.question: Epicurus taught that the gods do not exist.
quiz.explanation: Epicurus believed the gods exist and are perfectly blessed, but precisely because of that they do not interfere in the world, so there is no reason to fear them.

quiz.question: Epicurus advised his followers to avoid seeking political power and fame, summed up in the slogan 'live unnoticed'.
quiz.explanation: Since power and fame are empty desires that bring danger and anxiety, Epicureans generally preferred a quiet life among friends, which critics like Plutarch attacked.

quiz.question: Thomas Nagel's 'deprivation' objection holds that death can be bad for a person even though they never experience being dead.
quiz.explanation: Nagel argued that death is bad because it deprives us of goods we would otherwise have had, just as some harms are real even if we never learn of them.

goDeeper.body:
The Epicurean argument about death has generated one of the liveliest debates in modern philosophy. Thomas Nagel's 1970 essay 'Death' launched the **deprivation account**: death is bad for the one who dies because it takes away the goods of life they would otherwise have enjoyed. But this raises puzzles Epicurus was ready for. When exactly is death bad for you? Not while you are alive, since you are not yet dead; and not after, since you no longer exist. Philosophers such as Fred Feldman have answered that death's badness may be 'timeless', or located in the comparison between two possible lives, rather than at a moment. Others, including Stephen Rosenbaum, have defended Epicurus against Nagel.

The symmetry argument has its own literature. Derek Parfit pointed out that we are often biased toward the future: we care more about pain still to come than pain already past, even if the amounts are the same. If that bias is rational, Lucretius' mirror is distorted; if it is not, perhaps Lucretius was right after all.

Another debate concerns friendship. If an Epicurean values friends because they make life safe and pleasant, is that real friendship, or just useful association? Cicero pressed this objection hard in *On Ends* (*De Finibus*). Scholars such as Tim O'Keefe and David Konstan discuss how later Epicureans tried to show that friendship begins in utility but comes to be valued for its own sake, and whether a hedonist can consistently say this.

Finally, Epicurean physics had an extraordinary future. Pierre Gassendi in the seventeenth century revived Epicurean atomism in a form compatible with Christianity, and it fed into the 'mechanical philosophy' of the Scientific Revolution (Day 41).

readings.note: A philosopher's lively case for Epicureanism as a modern way of life, honest about its limits.

questions: Can a life of quiet pleasure among friends be fully good if it ignores politics and the wider world?
Is the deprivation account a convincing answer to Epicurus? Can something be bad for you if there is no time at which you experience it?
If you value a friend partly because they make your life pleasant, is that still real friendship?
